chapter_note: This chapter is overwhelmingly polemical, not expository. The title names a substrate topic (the two essences = primordial duality) but the chapter uses that topic as a weapon against monotheism rather than systematically mapping it. Mani is preaching/arguing, not teaching cosmological correspondences. The only substrate fragment is the brief naming of the two essences and their paired opposites in the opening paragraph. The remainder is direct argumentative address ('you'), rhetorical catalogues of evil, citations of Jesus's tree parable as proof-text, and eschatological warnings. Teaching purity 0.000 confirms this. No systematic mapping (face→realm, metal→body, taste→world) appears anywhere. The five trees are mentioned in ¶6 but as citation within polemic, not as expounded teaching. Heavy lacunae throughout make the chapter additionally fragmentary.

paragraphs.core_text: the two essences that are present at the beginning [ ... ] the light and the darkness, that which is good and that which is evi[], life and] death.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed dialogue frame opening: 'Once again, when our father looked, he saw a [ ... ] person [ ... ] before him. [He] says [ ... ]' — formulaic attribution with 'our father' honorific and narrative framing.
paragraphs.temporal_note: The naming of the two primordial essences with three paired opposites (light/darkness, good/evil, life/death) is a cosmological-correspondential statement — it maps the fundamental duality through parallel registers. This is the chapter's only cosmos→cosmos mapping. The rest of the chapter uses this claim polemically.

Direct address to 'you, however, the creatures' — argumentative rhetoric against monotheists. The cosmological claim (one vs. two essences) is being APPLIED to a contemporary theological debate, not being systematically taught. One side of the mapping reaches into the audience's religious position. Heavy lacunae obscure some content.

Rhetorical catalogue of evils directed at audience ('So, tell me...'). The list includes contemporary practices: 'worshipping of idols,' 'Mammon,' 'fornication in which people revel.' These are not systematic cosmic-domain mappings but a polemical inventory reaching into the contemporary moral world. The 'evil spirits that are like the night' approaches cosmic language but is embedded in the rhetorical frame. The question 'who cast them in the heart of people' is argumentative, not expository.

Continues the polemical argument via reductio ad absurdum: if evils came from God, why don't you do them? Direct 'you' address throughout. 'Two woes' and 'you forgive their sins' — argumentative rhetoric mapping cosmic claim→contemporary religious practice. No cosmological mapping present.

Continues argument. References 'his beloved son' and 'all the apostles' — institutional/apostolic authority claims. 'The bitter trees that give not fruit' and 'the hard earth' are citations of the tree parable (Gospel proof-text), not systematic cosmological teaching. Gardner confirms this is 'the favourite proof-text.' The vehicle is citation ('saying that'), not exposition. Heavy lacunae obscure the five-fold structure that Gardner notes.

'Once again he says' — citation formula. The 'five trees' reference is tantalizing (five-fold cosmological teaching exists as substrate elsewhere), but here it functions as proof-text within polemic, not as systematic teaching being expounded. 'His beloved son and his holy spirit and the entire kingdom' — theological/institutional language. The paragraph argues that attributing evil to God is blasphemous, using the tree teaching as evidence.

Eschatological warning/threat directed at audience: 'You will be condemned.' References 'his beloved son and his holy spirit at the last day, at his advent' — classic devotional-eschatological closure language. Direct address, future judgment, institutional theological vocabulary.

Final eschatological warning: 'You shall come from your body and see these things that I have recounted to you.' 'The Judge of truth, the one who shall not favour anyone' — devotional closure formula. First person ('I have recounted to you') anchors to the editorial Mani-as-speaker frame. Closes the polemical chapter with a judgment scene.
